summary: Defines a new BGP attribute, the Traffic Engineering attribute, that lets BGP carry traffic engineering information. Its scope currently excludes use for non-VPN reachability information.

plainLanguage.summary: BGP is how big networks tell each other about routes. This note adds a new field for passing along traffic planning hints with those route announcements.

subtitle: A new optional BGP attribute that lets VPN routes carry the traffic engineering details of a link.

tldr.problem: In some setups, such as Layer-1 VPNs, the reachability information that BGP carries is not enough, and it helps to attach traffic engineering information to it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5543 defines the Traffic Engineering attribute, an optional, non-transitive BGP attribute that carries the same data as the Interface Switching Capability Descriptor used in OSPF and IS-IS for GMPLS.
tldr.outcome: BGP can now carry per-interface capability data such as switching type, encoding, and maximum and minimum LSP bandwidth. Its scope currently excludes non-VPN reachability information, and it has since been updated by RFC 7606.

facts.label: Bandwidth units
facts.value: Bytes per second, IEEE floating point

today: RFC 5543 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7606. Its scope still excludes use of the attribute for non-VPN reachability information.

sections.title: Why BGP Needs a Traffic Engineering Attribute
sections.content:
In certain cases, for example Layer-1 VPNs (RFC 5195), it is useful to add Traffic Engineering information to the VPN reachability information that BGP already carries. RFC 5543 defines a new BGP attribute for this, so that BGP (RFC 4271) can carry that information.

The scope is deliberately narrow. The attribute currently may not be used for non-VPN reachability information. The procedures for modifying the attribute when a route that carries it is re-advertised are outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a route announcement needs a note saying how much traffic the path can handle. This RFC adds a place to write that note, but only for private network services.

sections.title: The Attribute and Its Fixed Fields
sections.content:
The Traffic Engineering attribute is an optional, non-transitive BGP attribute. The information inside is identical to what is carried in the Interface Switching Capability Descriptor defined in RFC 4203 and RFC 5307. The attribute holds one or more of these descriptors.

Each starts with a Switching Capability byte and an Encoding byte, both taking values from Section 3.1.1 of RFC 3471, then a 16-bit Reserved field. The reserved field SHOULD be set to 0 on transmit and MUST be ignored on receive.

Next come eight 4-octet Max LSP Bandwidth fields, for priority 0 first through priority 7 last. They use the IEEE floating point format, and the units are bytes (not bits) per second.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note starts with what kind of road it is, then lists the biggest load it can take for each of eight levels of importance.

sections.title: Switching Capability Specific Information
sections.content:
The last part of each descriptor is variable and depends on the Switching Capability field.

  • For PSC-1, PSC-2, PSC-3 or PSC-4, it holds a 4-octet Minimum LSP Bandwidth and a 2-octet Interface MTU.
  • For Layer-2 Switch Capable (L2SC), there is no specific information.
  • For Time-Division-Multiplex (TDM) capable, it holds a 4-octet Minimum LSP Bandwidth and a 1-octet indication of Standard or Arbitrary SONET/SDH. The value is 0 for Standard and 1 for Arbitrary.
  • For Lambda Switch Capable (LSC), there is no specific information.

Minimum LSP Bandwidth uses the same IEEE floating point format, in bytes per second. Interface MTU is a 2-octet integer.
sections.plainLanguage: After the main part, some kinds of road add extra details, like the smallest load allowed. Other kinds need nothing extra.

sections.title: Effect on Route Aggregation
sections.content:
Routes that carry the attribute have extra semantics that could affect how traffic is forwarded. Because of that, such routes SHALL NOT be aggregated unless they share identical Traffic Engineering attributes.

When routes with identical attributes are aggregated, the attribute for the aggregate is built following the procedure of RFC 4201.
sections.plainLanguage: You can only merge two route announcements into one if their notes about the road match exactly.

sections.title: Effect on Scalability
sections.content:
Using the attribute does not increase the number of routes, but it may increase the number of BGP Update messages needed to distribute them. That depends on whether the routes share the same attribute.

If routes differ in other ways, such as their Route Targets or NEXT_HOP, there is no impact on the number of Update messages. There is also no impact when routes share all other attribute information and have an aggregated or identical Traffic Engineering attribute. When routes share all other attribute information but have different Traffic Engineering attributes, they must be sent in per-route Update messages rather than in a single message.
sections.plainLanguage: If every route has a different note, they cannot travel in one big envelope, so more envelopes are needed.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA is told that this document defines a new BGP attribute named Traffic Engineering, which is optional and non-transitive.

On security, the extension does not change the underlying security issues already inherent in BGP. BGP security considerations are discussed in RFC 4271.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding the note does not make BGP any safer or any riskier than it already was.
